# kis (keep-in-secret)

> kis lets a team commit secret files (`.env` and any other path listed in
> `.gitencrypt`) to git **encrypted**. It is a git clean/smudge filter: `git add`
> encrypts, checkout decrypts, so the working copy is plaintext while the index,
> history and remote only hold ciphertext. Works with any language or stack.

Install (needs git 2.28+): `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juanfraherrero/keep-in-secret/main/install.sh | sh` (macOS/Linux), or `go install github.com/juanfraherrero/keep-in-secret/cmd/kis@latest`

## Rules for coding agents in a kis repository

A repository uses kis if it has a `.kis/` directory and a `.gitencrypt` file.

- Committing `.env` (and every file matched by `.gitencrypt`) is safe and expected.
  Do NOT add these files to `.gitignore`, `git rm` them, or move their values
  elsewhere to protect them. kis already does.
- `.env*.local` files are local: never commit them; don't remove them from
  `.gitignore`. They hold one developer's values, so kis doesn't encrypt them
  (the default `.gitencrypt` excludes them) and blocks committing them in
  plaintext: the pre-commit check refuses, and `kis status --check` fails.
- Before every push or pull request, run `kis status --check`. Exit 0 means safe
  to push; exit 1 means a secret would leave in plaintext, and the output prints
  the fix. For a pull request use `kis status --check --since origin/main`.
- "Safe to push" covers only files matched by `.gitencrypt`; kis does not scan
  other files for hardcoded secrets.
- Use `kis status --json` to read state as data. Fields: `initialized`,
  `safe_to_push`, `encrypted_files`, `unlocked`, `files[].state` (`encrypted`, `plaintext-index`,
  `plaintext-head`, `wrong-group`, `untracked`, `ignored`; plus `group`,
  `readable`), `groups[]`, `you` (the partner this machine acts as; absent when
  no key here has access) with `your_key`, and `problems[]` with `severity`
  (`error` blocks a push, `warning` does not), `path`, `commit`, `message`, `fix`.
- To encrypt another file: add its path to `.gitencrypt` (gitignore syntax), then
  run `kis sync`. Never edit the kis block of `.gitattributes` by hand.
- A secret file that is binary and starts with the bytes `\0KIS\0v1\0` means
  this clone is locked. `kis unlock` needs the developer's private key; ask
  them rather than working around it.
- In a fresh clone, run `kis unlock` first, even without a key: it sets git up
  so secret files can't be committed in plaintext (`git add` then refuses a
  secret file holding plaintext: `refusing to store FILE in plaintext:
  repository is locked`). If it says you have no access, leave secret files
  alone and ask the developer.
- Which private key kis uses, the same in every command (`init`, `unlock`,
  `pubkey`, and `sync` / `add` when they create a group); first match wins:
  1. `--identity PATH` (a private key file; only that file),
  2. `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY` (the key's text, not a path; key files are ignored),
  3. `$KIS_IDENTITY`, `~/.config/kis/identity`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`,
     `~/.ssh/id_rsa`.
  A set but unusable source is an error, never a fallback. `kis pubkey` and
  the `unlock` message say which key was used.
- Never run `kis keygen --force` yourself: it replaces the developer's key, and
  their repositories still only know the old one. Ask the developer.
- If the developer's private key is not in a standard place, pass
  `--identity PATH` to each of those commands, where PATH is their **private**
  key file (ask them for the path; never guess or search for keys). kis does
  not remember it; the developer can set `KIS_IDENTITY=PATH` instead.
- On CI or a cloud agent, kis reads the private key from the `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY`
  environment variable. If it is missing, ask the developer to run
  `kis add NAME --new-key` and store the printed key as that secret; never
  move secret values into the platform's own variables to bypass kis. Several
  agents: one `kis add agent-N --new-key` per agent, each key in that agent's
  own secret, so one can be revoked alone. Never print those keys into logs,
  commits or chat.
- `kis add NAME --new-key` writes only the private key, on one line, to stdout;
  every message goes to stderr. Run it yourself only piped straight into the
  platform's secret store (as `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY`), so you never read the key;
  the command for that depends on the platform. If you can't pipe it there,
  ask the developer to run it.
- `kis init` with `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY` set uses that key as the first partner
  and writes no key file. Without a terminal it warns when its key is the only
  partner: tell the developer, and add them (`kis add NAME KEY`) before
  pushing, so the repository doesn't depend on a disposable machine.
- A line ending in `@GROUP` (e.g. `.env.production @prod`) encrypts those files
  for that group only. Files of a group this clone isn't in stay ciphertext:
  that is expected, commit around them; never try to decrypt or recreate them.
  Access: `kis add NAME --group GROUP` (run by a member of that group).
  `--group` takes one group; run the command once per group.
- Don't copy secret values into code, logs, commit messages, PRs or chat. If a
  task seems to need one, refer to the variable by name, or ask the developer.

## Setting kis up (non-interactive)

Every prompt takes its default without a terminal; `-y` forces it.

```sh
kis init -y --name NAME              # creates .gitencrypt, key, AGENTS.md section
                                     # NAME: how partners will see the developer (committed);
                                     # without --name, the git email before the @ is used
git commit -m "Set up kis encryption" && git push
kis add PARTNER age1…|github:USER|key.pub   # then commit and push
kis unlock                           # partner, after cloning
kis add ci --new-key [--group G]     # CI / cloud agent: stdout is the key; pipe it into the secret KIS_PRIVATE_KEY
KIS_PRIVATE_KEY=… kis unlock         # on that machine
```

## Choosing which files to encrypt

Find the project's secret files, add their paths to `.gitencrypt`, run
`kis sync`; [gitencrypt-patterns.md](https://github.com/juanfraherrero/keep-in-secret/blob/main/docs/gitencrypt-patterns.md)
lists common ones per stack (Android keystores, Rails keys, Spring profiles,
Terraform variables). Ask the developer when unsure: encrypting a file CI reads
in plaintext breaks CI until CI runs `kis unlock`. A pattern with a slash only
matches at the repository root; use `**/` to match at any depth (monorepos).

## Commands

- `kis init [--identity PATH] [--name NAME] [--no-agents] [-y]`: set up encryption
- `kis status [--check] [--json] [--since REV]`: state and whether it is safe to push
- `kis sync [--identity PATH]`: apply `.gitencrypt` edits and re-encrypt
- `kis add NAME [KEY|github:USER|FILE.pub|--new-key] [--group G] [--identity PATH]`: give a partner access, optionally to a group; `--new-key` makes a key for CI or a cloud agent. `github:USER` grants access to every ed25519/RSA key on that GitHub account, read once; for a single key, ask the person for it
- `kis remove NAME [--group G] [--no-rotate]`: revoke and rotate the affected keys
- `kis rotate [--group G]`: new key(s), re-encrypt
- `kis unlock [--identity PATH]` (or `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY`) / `kis lock [--force]`: decrypt / re-encrypt this clone
- `kis keygen [--force [-y]]`: create the developer's age key, or print it if it exists. `--force` replaces it (the old one becomes `identity.bak`; an older backup is deleted only after a prompt or `-y`), and repositories then still only know the old key
- `kis pubkey [--identity PATH]`: personal key management (`pubkey` prints the keys kis uses here and where each comes from). Accepted keys: age (`age1…`), SSH ed25519, SSH RSA; ECDSA and security keys (`sk-`) are refused
